name: task-runner-ultimate
description: Task and script explorer with one list in your monorepo: package.json, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, Makefile, justfile, Taskfile and more. Batch & single run, stop and restart from anywhere, with a live count of what's running.

taskRunnerUltimate.title.description: Heading over the list, in the activity bar view and in the File Explorer section alike. 1 to 100 characters; left empty it falls back to "Task & Script Explorer". The tooltip on the activity bar icon itself is fixed when the extension is installed and keeps the extension's name.

enumDescriptions: Detect from the packageManager field, the engines field, then lock and config files.
taskRunnerUltimate.packageManager.description: Runner used for package.json scripts. Tasks from deno.json(c) always use 'deno task' regardless of this setting, and no other ecosystem is affected.

taskRunnerUltimate.showInStatusBar.description: Also show a 'Task & Script Explorer' entry in the status bar.

taskRunnerUltimate.showInEditorTitle.description: Show the scripts icon in the editor title bar.

taskRunnerUltimate.showInFileExplorer.description: Also show the task list as a section at the bottom of the File Explorer.

taskRunnerUltimate.openDropdownFromActiv.description: Also open the dropdown when the Task & Script Explorer view in the activity bar is revealed. Off by default: the view already shows the same list as a tree.

taskRunnerUltimate.exclude.description: Glob pattern of manifest locations to ignore while scanning.

enumDescriptions: pyproject.toml (poetry, pdm, hatch, rye, poe), Pipfile, tox.ini and noxfile.py.
docker-compose.yml, compose.yml and their .yaml spellings — the compose subcommands.
Shell scripts (.sh, .bash, .zsh, .ksh, .ps1, .bat, .cmd) under scripts/, bin/ and the workspace root.

taskRunnerUltimate.sources.markdownDescription: Which kinds of manifest are scanned. Remove an entry to stop reading that ecosystem entirely — the files are then never opened, which is also the fastest way to quieten a repository that carries a `Makefile` nobody runs.

taskRunnerUltimate.cargoCommands.markdownDescription:
Cargo subcommands listed for every `Cargo.toml`, since a crate declares no scripts of its own. Known names (`build`, `test`, `check`, `clippy`, `fmt`, `bench`, `doc`, `clean`, `update`) get their usual flags; anything else runs as `cargo <name>`.

`run` is special: it expands to what the crate can actually run — nothing for a library, one row per `[[bin]]` for a crate with several, plus a row per example.

taskRunnerUltimate.goCommands.markdownDescription: Go subcommands listed for every `go.mod`. Known names are `run`, `build`, `test`, `vet`, `fmt`, `tidy`, `generate` and `bench`; anything else runs as `go <name>`. `run` is dropped for a module whose root is not itself a program.

enumDescriptions: Detect from the lock file beside pyproject.toml, then from the [tool.*] table it configures.
taskRunnerUltimate.pythonRunner.markdownDescription: How `[project.scripts]` entry points are entered. Tasks that name their own runner — `[tool.pdm.scripts]`, `[tool.poetry.scripts]` and the rest — ignore this.

enumDescriptions: The v2 plugin, which is what a current Docker installs.
The standalone v1 binary, end-of-life since July 2023.
taskRunnerUltimate.dockerCompose.markdownDescription:
How compose is invoked. Spelled as the command and split on whitespace, so what is written here is what reaches the terminal.

There is no `auto`: the only honest way to tell the two apart is to run `docker compose version`, and a scan never starts a process.

Machine-scoped, as `#taskRunnerUltimate.shellRunner#` and `#taskRunnerUltimate.shellRunners#` are: the value is run as a program rather than typed into a task terminal, so a repository’s own `.vscode/settings.json` cannot choose it for you.

taskRunnerUltimate.dockerComposeCommands.markdownDescription:
Compose subcommands listed for every compose file, since a compose file declares services rather than tasks. Known names (`up`, `down`, `build`, `logs`, `ps`, `start`, `stop`, `restart`, `pull`, `config`) get their usual flags — `logs` is followed, so the row keeps running — and anything else runs as `docker compose <name>`.

`up` is special: it lists a bare row for the whole file plus one `up: <service>` row per service, whenever the file declares more than one.

Nothing here is ever run detached. A `-d` row would exit the moment it started, leaving the containers up and Stop with nothing to stop.

Every row passes `-f <file>`. For the four names compose picks by itself — `compose.yaml`, `compose.yml`, `docker-compose.yaml`, `docker-compose.yml` — a second `-f` is added for the first of compose’s own four override names beside it (`compose.override.yaml`, `compose.override.yml`, `docker-compose.override.yaml`, `docker-compose.override.yml`), which is the merge compose would have done. A profile-named file such as `docker-compose.dev.yml` gets none: that merge is something compose does to the file it chose for itself. No file with `.override.` in its name is ever a heading of its own.

Profile-named compose files (`docker-compose.dev.yml`, `compose.prod.yaml`) are found too, and each is a heading of its own. One of those is only believed once it shows a `services:` or `include:` block, since nothing inside a YAML file otherwise says that it is compose.

taskRunnerUltimate.shellScripts.markdownDescription:
Where shell scripts are looked for, as globs matched against each file’s path **relative to its workspace folder**. Every script found becomes a row, and in `flat` grouping the ones a project holds are drawn together under a single `shell` heading.

The leading `**/` is what carries the first two past the root: without it a `scripts` folder would have to sit at the very top, and `apps/web/scripts/deploy.sh` would never be found. The third pattern keeps no prefix on purpose, so loose scripts are listed where a project root is rather than in every directory.

Seven extensions: the Bourne family (`.sh`, `.bash`, `.zsh`, `.ksh`) and the three Windows writes its scripts in (`.ps1`, `.bat`, `.cmd`). Which one a file carries decides the words it is run through — see `#taskRunnerUltimate.shellRunners#` — and the terminal glyph its row wears. A `{a,b}` group works in a pattern of your own too.

The executable bit is deliberately not consulted: it is invisible to VS Code’s own file API, and reading it would mean giving up Remote SSH and Dev Containers. The convention — a script under `scripts`, under `bin`, or in the root — is the signal instead.

At most 200 scripts are read, budgeted apart from the manifests. Narrow these patterns if a repository has more.

taskRunnerUltimate.shellRunner.markdownDescription:
What a Bourne-family shell row — `.sh`, `.bash`, `.zsh`, `.ksh` — is run through, from the workspace folder root: `bash ./scripts/deploy.sh`. Leave empty to run the path on its own, which then needs both the executable bit and a shebang.

On Windows this wants Git Bash or WSL on the `PATH`. The Windows extensions are started by `#taskRunnerUltimate.shellRunners#` instead.

Machine-scoped, like `#taskRunnerUltimate.dockerCompose#`: this value is run as a program rather than typed into a task terminal, so a repository’s own `.vscode/settings.json` cannot choose it for you.

taskRunnerUltimate.shellRunners.markdownDescription:
What each extension is run through, keyed by extension — the map that covers what `#taskRunnerUltimate.shellRunner#` does not. An extension that appears here is started with these words in front of the path; one that does not falls back to `shellRunner`.

`powershell` and not `pwsh`: Windows PowerShell 5.1 ships with the OS, where PowerShell 7 is an install away. On 7, set `pwsh -NoProfile -File`. If an execution policy blocks the script, `powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File` is the usual answer — deliberately not the default.

`.bat` and `.cmd` are run as themselves, with no runner at all: they are programs to Windows already, and the PowerShell a task starts in takes the `./path/to/x.bat` this builds. With `cmd.exe` as the terminal profile, set `cmd /c` for both.

Machine-scoped, like `#taskRunnerUltimate.dockerCompose#`: this value is run as a program rather than typed into a task terminal, so a repository’s own `.vscode/settings.json` cannot choose it for you.

taskRunnerUltimate.colorIcons.description: Tint script icons in the Task & Script Explorer view with their category colour. Turn off to keep every icon in the default foreground colour.

taskRunnerUltimate.pinRunningTasks.description: Show running tasks first inside the group they belong to, in the tree and in the dropdown alike. Off by default: a row that stays put is a row you stop where you started it.

enumDescriptions: One row per manifest, with compose files and script folders inside the project they serve.
One row per ecosystem, with that ecosystem’s manifests inside it.
taskRunnerUltimate.grouping.markdownDescription:
How the package headings are arranged, in the tree and in the dropdown alike.

`flat` keeps one row per manifest and folds each compose file and script folder in under the nearest project above it, so the infrastructure of a package sits inside that package.

`ecosystem` gathers the manifests of each language or runner under a row of their own — there a compose file is filed under Docker rather than under the package it serves, because that is the question that mode answers.

Also in the view's header, as a button that names the mode it puts you in, and on the ☰ menu as **Group by ecosystem**.

enumDescriptions: Each heading wears the icon its own file has in your file icon theme.
Every heading wears the same stack glyph.
taskRunnerUltimate.groupIcons.markdownDescription:
What a package heading is drawn with. `type` asks your **file icon theme** for the icon that manifest has in the Explorer — the real npm, Rust and Docker marks, which no icon font carries; a folder of shell scripts has no file for a theme to match on, so it wears a terminal. `uniform` is the quieter column the tree used to have, for when the headings should stay out of the way of the rows under them.

The colour is separate either way: a heading is tinted when you paint it, and the tint lands on the text and leaves the icon its own colours. An icon picked by hand on a row wins over both.

Ecosystem rows are not covered — they name no file, so they keep their own glyph in both modes. Nor is a `shell` heading that stands for several folders, which is the same kind of row.

taskRunnerUltimate.categories.markdownDescription:
Extra category rules, checked **before** the built-in ones (run, stop, test, quality, build, release, data, clean), so a single entry can override a built-in. Each rule matches the script name token by token, then the command it runs.

```json
[{ "match": ["bench", "perf"], "icon": "dashboard", "color": "charts.purple" }]
```

`icon` is a codicon id, `color` a theme colour id — either one of `taskRunnerUltimate.category.*` or any built-in such as `charts.green`.
